title: Other paths
hookLine: the Gurus respected sincere seekers of every path and defended their freedom

lines: A GURU WHO GAVE HIS LIFE FOR OTHERS.
cards: Open the Guru Granth Sahib toward its last pages and you meet a name that isn't a Guru's: Sheikh Farid, a Sufi, a Muslim mystic, his verses kept right there in the Sikh scripture.
Elsewhere you find Kabir the weaver, Namdev the calico printer, Ravidas the leatherworker. Their hymns sit beside the Gurus' own and are bowed to in the same way.
That alone says something about how the Gurus saw people on other paths. But they went further than keeping their words. One Guru gave his life for people whose path was not his own.

teach.h: THE BHAGATS' HYMNS KEPT IN THE GRANTH.
teach.b: First, the voices kept. You met the Bhagats early on this path: saints from Hindu and Muslim backgrounds whose hymns the Granth gathers beside the Gurus'. What it keeps is their devotion, not their birth or their label.
Second, the living, not the label.

teach.h: MAJH: HARD TO TRULY BE A MUSLIM.
teach.b: In a salok in Majh ki Var, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase: it's hard to be called a Muslim; only one who truly is one should be called that.
Then he describes truly being one: the way of the saints sweet to you, pride scraped away like rust, kindness to all. He doesn't mock the faith. He sets its bar high, from inside its own words.

teach.h: GURU TEGH BAHADUR: THEIR THREAD, THEIR TILAK.
teach.b: Guru Gobind Singh's Bachitar Natak says of his father, Guru Tegh Bahadur, in paraphrase: he protected their tilak and their sacred thread.

teach.h: A WEEK THAT WIDENS THE CIRCLE.
teach.b: Sikhs remember that Kashmiri Pandits, Hindus under pressure to convert, came to the Guru for help, and that he went to Delhi and was executed there. Sikhs don't wear the tilak or the thread.
He died for other people's right to wear them. Fourth, the week. Work as worship.
Wealth earned and shared. Equal souls. Women as equals.
Peace first. Stand for others. Each one widens the circle.
Respect the sincere isn't saying every path is identical, and it isn't keeping score. It's noticing a person who truly seeks, and honoring that, whatever name they pray in.

how: The Guru Granth Sahib includes hymns by Bhagats from Hindu and Muslim backgrounds, such as Kabir and Sheikh Farid; Sikhs remember Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom as a defense of the freedom of religion.

o: a belief that every religion teaches the same thing
honoring sincere seekers, whatever name they pray in
a duty to bring people of other faiths to the Gurus

p: a Sufi whose verses are in the Granth
Guru Nanak in Majh ki Var
hard to truly be called a Muslim
saints whose hymns sit beside the Gurus'

s: the Guru Granth Sahib holds only the Gurus' own hymns
it keeps the Bhagats too: Kabir, Namdev, Ravidas, Sheikh Farid.
Guru Tegh Bahadur defended a freedom for people of another path
the Bachitar Natak says he protected their tilak and sacred thread.
Guru Nanak's Majh salok mocks Muslims
it sets the bar high from inside the faith: truly being one is hard.

games.q: you're Guru Tegh Bahadur. people of another faith, under pressure to convert, come asking for help. what do you do?
o: tell them it's not your community's concern.
stand for their freedom, at any cost.
invite them to become Sikhs instead.
games.why: Sikhs remember that he went to Delhi and was executed, defending a freedom he didn't need for himself.

practice: Bring to mind someone whose path is different from yours: a coworker who fasts, a neighbor who goes to services, a friend who prays in another language, or one who doesn't pray at all and still searches.
Breathe in and see their sincerity, the early mornings, the questions they carry. Breathe out and let your respect for it be quiet and real.

wordCard.voice: Other paths. The Gurus kept the hymns of saints from other backgrounds in the Granth, and Guru Tegh Bahadur died defending the freedom of people whose path was not his. Today's word.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: bhagat, a devotee; the Bhagats are the saints whose hymns sit in the Granth beside the Gurus'.

carryVoice: Your line: respect the sincere. The circle keeps widening. See you on the path tomorrow.

sources.ref: Ang 141 (Majh ki Var, salok of Guru Nanak)
Bachitar Natak (Guru Gobind Singh), on Guru Tegh Bahadur
